en: The Jātaka:
The Eighth Chapter, The Section on Kaccāyana (Aṭṭhakanipāta Kaccānivagga)
7. The Indriya Jātaka:
“O Nārada, he who, out of desire for the sense-faculties, falls under their control;”
Thus, having abandoned both worlds,
he withers away even while still living;
after happiness comes suffering.
After suffering comes happiness; having tasted suffering for the sake of happiness,
one may expect superior happiness as the result.
In times of hardship,
the wise person who endures hardship and does not yield to it finds happiness at the very end of that hardship.
One attains yoga. It is not for the sake of sensual pleasures, nor for various harmful things,
nor for the purpose of causing harm.
“Without disregarding what has been done,
you ought not to deviate from the Dhamma.
“It is good, householder, that you see clearly;”
And sharing food; being free from dejection when gains are lost,
and remaining unperturbed when misfortune strikes.”
“This much is his wisdom,” so said Devila;
“there is nothing worse than this.”
"He who falls under the power of the senses,
Sivi, will come to me as if falling into the very hands of his enemies."
One should observe one's duty, knowledge,
skill, marriage, virtue, and gentleness; yet having neglected these,
one’s fame shall perish.
Reborn through my own deeds,
I am a thousand-liver,
friendless and without refuge.
Having departed from the noble Dhamma,
I am just like a peta;
having caused those who desire happiness to suffer, [I have brought this upon myself].
I have fallen into this state;
I find no happiness,
standing as if in the midst of a blazing fire.
The Indriya Jātaka is the seventh.
